recipe.history:
Asiago is one of the great cheeses of the Veneto region of northeastern Italy, produced in the high alpine meadows of the Asiago plateau in the provinces of Vicenza and Trento, where dairy farmers have been making cheese from the milk of their mountain cattle since at least the 10th century. The cheese takes its name from the town of Asiago and exists in two principal forms: 'Asiago Pressato,' a young, mild, ivory-white cheese aged for a few weeks that melts beautifully and has a buttery, slightly sweet flavor; and 'Asiago d'Allevo,' an aged version that ranges from medium-sharp at a few months to intensely granular and pungent at over a year, developing a firm texture similar to Parmesan and a nutty, complex flavor with notable crystalline crunch. Both forms have held protected designation of origin (DOP) status from the European Union since 1996, meaning that authentic Asiago can only be produced in a specific geographic area under strict rules. The cheese's dual nature — mild and melting when young, bold and crystalline when aged — makes it unusually versatile in the kitchen.

Asiago arrived in American cuisine through Italian-American cooking, where it was often used as a Parmesan substitute or shredded over pasta, salads, and soups. Its transition to burger culture came through the artisan cheese movement of the 2000s, when restaurant chefs began exploring the full range of cow's milk cheeses as burger toppings beyond American, Swiss, and cheddar. Asiago's combination of good melt (when younger) and bold, nutty flavor (from aged shards) made it particularly interesting on burgers: a thin layer of young Asiago melted over the hot patty, crowned with paper-thin shavings of aged Asiago that stayed distinct and added texture, created a layered cheese experience that no single-type cheese application could achieve. The play between melted and shaved became a technique in itself.

I encountered Asiago seriously at a small Italian deli that opened near my apartment years ago. The owner kept a wedge of aged Asiago on the counter and would shave pieces of it onto whatever you were buying — sandwiches, crackers, soup — with a sort of casual generosity that made you feel like you were being given something valuable. I started buying the young Asiago to melt and the aged Asiago to shave, and eventually I started putting both on burgers. The first time I tried it I understood immediately why it worked: the melted young Asiago added a creamy, buttery layer that amplified the beef fat, and the shaved aged Asiago on top added sharp, crystalline punctuation. It was a burger that kept changing as you ate it.

Asiago cheese — nutty, rich, and in its aged form almost aggressively savory — demands a medium rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 Celsius, because the cheese's boldness requires the full flavor of properly cooked beef to match it. Well-done beef, stripped of its moisture and rendered fat, becomes a neutral background that the Asiago overwhelms; the burger tastes like melted cheese on bread with a gray disk of protein. Medium rare beef has the mineral intensity, the fat, and the juice to stand beside aged Asiago as an equal. The Asiago does not overwhelm the beef; the beef does not disappear behind the cheese. They negotiate. That negotiation is what makes the burger worth eating.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
1/2 tsp dried Italian herb blend (oregano, basil, thyme)
200g young (fresh/pressed) Asiago cheese, thinly sliced for melting
80g aged Asiago cheese, shaved into thin shards with a vegetable peeler
instructions: 1. Make the roasted garlic aioli: Preheat oven to 400°F (200°C). Slice the top 1/4 inch off the head of garlic to expose the cloves. Drizzle with olive oil, wrap in foil, and roast for 40 to 45 minutes until the cloves are golden, soft, and fragrant. Squeeze the roasted garlic from its skins into a small bowl and mash to a paste. Combine with mayonnaise, lemon juice, black pepper, and salt. Whisk until smooth. Refrigerate until needed.

2. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead with dough hook on medium for 8 minutes until smooth. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.

3. Divide into 4 equal portions, shape into smooth balls, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash, sprinkle sesame seeds, and bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool completely.

4. Shave the aged Asiago: Using a sharp vegetable peeler or a sharp knife, shave the aged Asiago into thin, irregular shards. Set aside at room temperature. Slice the young Asiago into thin, even pieces for melting.

5. Shape patties: Combine ground beef, salt, black pepper, garlic powder, and Italian herb blend. Mix gently and divide into 4 equal portions. Shape into patties 3/4 inch thick and slightly wider than the buns. Press a dimple into the center of each.
6. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties undisturbed for 3 minutes.

7. Flip patties and immediately layer slices of young Asiago over each. Cook 2 to 3 more minutes, checking temperature. Add a splash of water to the skillet and cover briefly to help the cheese melt. Remove patties at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Tent with foil and rest 3 to 4 minutes.
8. Toast buns cut-side down in residual skillet fat for 60 to 90 seconds until golden.

9. Assemble: Spread roasted garlic aioli generously on both cut sides of the bun. Place green leaf lettuce on the bottom bun, followed by tomato slices and red onion. Set the patty with melted young Asiago on top. Crown generously with shaved aged Asiago shards. Close the bun and serve immediately.
